--- title: "Championships: NBA and WNBA eras" --- ::: {.callout-important appearance="simple"} ## Why the time windows differ - **NBA section:** **2005-06 to 2025-26**, starting with the first season that has salaries reported for about 99% of minutes. - **WNBA section:** every WNBA season we have, **2009 to 2026**. WNBA salary records start only in 2021, and starting there would leave six champions to learn from. - **NBA vs WNBA:** the two leagues are compared season against season, never pooled. - **Models that learn from champions use all of each league's seasons in its window.** There is one champion per season, so a short window leaves too few champions to test a model. - **Shot zones are calibrated by season.** ESPN's recorded shot positions drift between eras, most visibly in the WNBA's 2020 bubble season, so the rim zone is anchored to where layups are recorded each season (Data page). ::: ::: {#takeaways .cell execution_count=2} ::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"} ## Takeaways - **NBA playoffs punish threes and rim attempts.** Points per three fell in the playoffs in 100% of NBA seasons since 2005-06 (-0.040 per shot); rim attempts in 90%. Mid-range shots held up best. - **WNBA playoffs:** no shot zone shows a reliable playoff change; with 8-12 playoff teams a year the sample is small. - **WNBA 2026's shot mix most resembles the NBA in 2018-19** on three-point share, which points to which NBA champions to study (below). - **Recent champions vs their own league (2022-26):** WNBA champions +5.3 points of shots from three and -6.3 at the rim; NBA champions +2.3 and -0.7. - **Net rating plus our availability-adjusted strength predicts NBA playoff series better than net rating alone** (74% vs 70% called correctly). ::: ::: # NBA (2005-06 to 2025-26) ## NBA: which shots survive the playoffs? ```{=html}
``` **What this shows:** bars left of zero are shots that get worse in the playoffs; the whiskers are 95% intervals. In the NBA, three, rim, paint / short mid, long mid reliably lose value, with **three** losing the most (-0.040 points per shot, worse in 100% of seasons). Shots that cross zero hold up about as well as in the regular season. ## NBA: are champions leaning toward threes? ```{=html}
``` **What this shows:** the gray line is the share of NBA shots that were threes each season; the dots are that season's champion. Over the last five seasons, 3 of 5 champions took more threes than the league, by +2.3 points on average, against +1.9 in the seasons before. ## NBA: champion identity ```{=html}
``` **What this shows:** each dot is an NBA champion. Right = better offense than the league that season, up = better defense. Identity comes from the gap between the two edges (points per 100 possessions): within 2 = *balanced*, 2-5 = *defense-* or *offense-leaning*, 5 or more = *defense-* or *offense-first*. Counts of NBA champions: 1 defense-first, 5 defense-leaning, 9 balanced, 6 offense-leaning, 0 offense-first. Recent champions: GS 2022: defense-leaning; DEN 2023: offense-leaning; BOS 2024: offense-leaning; OKC 2025: balanced; NY 2026: balanced. **How to read these tables:** every number is the champions' average minus the league average that season, in percentage points of team minutes or shots. +5 means the champions gave 5 points more of their minutes (or shots) to that role than the average team did; 0 means they looked like everyone else. *Champions* is the number of title teams in that era. This is not a measure of one league being "behind" the other. For each WNBA season, it finds the NBA season whose shot mix is the same, so we can look at what won in that NBA season and ask whether the same patterns show up in the WNBA. ```{=html}
``` | WNBA season | closest NBA season | NBA champion then | WNBA champion | |--------------:|:---------------------|:----------------------|:----------------------| | 2019 | 2015-16 | CLE (offense-leaning) | WSH (offense-first) | | 2020 | 2016-17 | GS (balanced) | SEA (defense-leaning) | | 2021 | 2016-17 | GS (balanced) | CHI (balanced) | | 2022 | 2017-18 | GS (offense-leaning) | LV (offense-first) | | 2023 | 2016-17 | GS (balanced) | LV (offense-first) | | 2024 | 2017-18 | GS (offense-leaning) | NY (balanced) | | 2025 | 2018-19 | TOR (balanced) | LV (balanced) | | 2026 | 2019-20 | LAL (defense-leaning) | GS (defense-first) | **Is the WNBA standing still in one NBA era, or moving through them?** It is moving. On three-point share, in 2009-13 it looked like the NBA of about 2012-13 (the NBA's 2011-16 era); in 2014-17 it looked like the NBA of about 2011-12 (the NBA's 2011-16 era); in 2018-21 it looked like the NBA of about 2015-16 (the NBA's 2011-16 era); in 2022-26 it looked like the NBA of about 2017-18 (the NBA's 2017-21 era). Over the last seven WNBA seasons the matching NBA season has advanced about **0.5 NBA seasons per WNBA season**: slower than one-for-one, so the WNBA is moving through the NBA's eras rather than standing still in one, while the NBA keeps moving too. Its champions are already ahead of it: recent WNBA champions took more threes and gave more minutes to 3-and-D wings than their league, the way NBA champions did before the NBA's shift. **What this shows:** both lines rise together: as the WNBA has taken more threes and fewer mid-range shots, the NBA season it resembles has moved forward too, and by 2026 it matches the NBA of about 2019-20 on threes. The table pairs each recent WNBA season with its closest NBA season and both champions. Where the identities line up (for example balanced champions in both), the NBA's later seasons are a reasonable guide to what the WNBA may reward next; where they differ, the WNBA is following its own path. ## Shot mix, both leagues ```{=html}
``` **What this shows:** both leagues are moving the same direction (more threes, fewer mid-range shots), the NBA earlier and faster. The WNBA's mid-range share has fallen most since 2020. ::: {.caveat} Association, not causation. Each league is measured against itself; NBA and WNBA numbers are compared, never pooled. :::
